lead: DSRC (dedicated short-range communications) is the radio service for road safety in the 5.9 GHz band. IEEE 802.11p is its lower layers: Wi-Fi changed for fast-moving cars, with 10 MHz channels and no joining handshake before sending. WAVE (wireless access in vehicular environments, the IEEE 1609 family) sits above 802.11p and handles channel switching, short-message networking and security. Together they let a car broadcast a basic safety message about ten times a second to every car and roadside unit within a few hundred metres. Only a few universities teach this stack in depth.
prereq: You need V2X communication and the routing ideas of VANETs.

blocks.text: In the USA the DSRC band was 5.850 to 5.925 GHz, seven 10 MHz channels: one control channel (CCH), channel 178, and six service channels (SCH). In 2020 the US regulator gave the lower 45 MHz to unlicensed Wi-Fi and the upper 30 MHz (5.895 to 5.925 GHz) to cellular V2X, so new US systems are moving away from DSRC. Europe's ITS-G5, built on the same 802.11p radio, uses channels between 5.855 and 5.925 GHz.

The 802.11p physical layer uses OFDM, like 802.11a, but with the clock halved: 10 MHz channels instead of 20 MHz, so every symbol is twice as long (8 µs). The longer guard time tolerates the echoes and Doppler shift of a moving car, and the data rates halve to 3 to 27 Mbit/s; 6 Mbit/s is the usual rate for safety messages. The MAC runs outside the context of a basic service set (OCB): a car does not scan, join, authenticate or exchange keys with an access point before sending. It listens for a free channel and broadcasts. EDCA (enhanced distributed channel access) gives four access categories, so safety frames wait a shorter time before sending than ordinary data. The radio is half duplex: it cannot send and receive on one channel at once.

items: IEEE 1609.2, security: signs messages with certificates from a public-key infrastructure, and can encrypt them, so a receiver can check the sender and that the message was not changed. It sits beside the other layers and serves them all.

IEEE 1609.3, networking services: WSMP (WAVE short message protocol) carries small safety packets with very little header; WAVE service advertisements tell cars which service is on which channel; ordinary internet traffic uses IPv6 with UDP or TCP.

IEEE 1609.4, multi-channel operation: a 100 ms sync interval, timed from GNSS, is split into a CCH interval and an SCH interval, normally 50 ms each with a short guard time at each switch. Every single-radio car is on the control channel at the same time, for safety messages and advertisements, and goes to a service channel for other data.
IEEE 1609.1, resource manager: an application-level service that let a remote application use an OBU's resources; it was little used and later withdrawn, so most stacks leave it out.

blocks.text: The common safety message is the basic safety message (BSM) of SAE J2735: position, speed, heading, acceleration, brake status and vehicle size, sent about ten times a second, typically 200 to 400 bytes with its security data.

examples.question: A 300-byte BSM is sent at 6 Mbit/s. Ignoring the preamble and MAC header, how long is one transmission, and how many such messages fit into one 50 ms control-channel interval if 10 per cent of the interval is lost to guard time and contention? How many cars, each sending one BSM per 100 ms sync interval, could share the channel at best?
steps: Usable part of the CCH interval: 50 ms × (1 − 0.10) = 45 ms.
Each car sends one BSM per 100 ms, which is one per CCH interval, so at best 112 cars can share the channel.
examples.answer: One BSM takes 0.4 ms; 112 fit in a 45 ms usable interval, so about 112 cars at best; preambles, headers and collisions lower this in a real jam.

traps: 802.11p uses 10 MHz channels, not the 20 MHz of 802.11a, so its symbols are twice as long and its rates are half.
WAVE is not another name for 802.11p: 802.11p is only the MAC and physical layer; WAVE is the IEEE 1609 layers above it.
The 100 ms sync interval is the channel-switching rhythm of 1609.4; it does not mean only one BSM fits in it.
3 to 27 Mbit/s is the raw physical rate; delivered throughput in a crowded channel is much lower.

quiz.q: What band and channel width does DSRC use, and which channel is the control channel in the US plan?
quiz.a: The 5.9 GHz band, 10 MHz channels; channel 178 is the control channel.

quiz.q: Why can an 802.11p car send without associating to an access point?
quiz.a: It works outside a basic service set (OCB), so there is no scan, join or key exchange; a safety message cannot wait for a handshake with cars that are only in range for seconds.

quiz.q: A 200-byte frame is sent at 3 Mbit/s. Find its airtime.
Name the IEEE 1609 standards and one job of each.
quiz.a: 1609.2 security (signatures, certificates); 1609.3 networking (WSMP, service advertisements, IPv6); 1609.4 multi-channel timing (CCH and SCH intervals); 1609.1 resource manager (little used, withdrawn).

quiz.q: Why does 1609.4 alternate the control and service channels?
quiz.a: A car with one radio can be on only one channel at a time. Switching all cars together, timed by GNSS, guarantees that every car is on the control channel at the same moment for safety messages, while still letting it use service channels for other data.

quiz.q: Why are 802.11p's rates half those of 802.11a?
quiz.a: The channel is 10 MHz instead of 20 MHz, so each OFDM symbol lasts 8 µs instead of 4 µs; the same modulation carries half the bits per second, but the longer guard time copes with road echoes.

beyond: Not for the exam. IEEE 802.11bd is the successor of 802.11p, with better coding and higher rates, and 5G NR-V2X is its cellular rival. Security work centres on 1609.2 certificates, pseudonyms and revocation lists. Search for IEEE 802.11bd, ETSI ITS-G5 and SAE J2735.
